quals-wisconsin-algebra-2006s-01.title: Modular law and trivial intersections
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2006s-01.body:
Distinct minimal normal subgroups $X\ne Y$ satisfy $X\cap Y=1$: $X\cap Y\trianglelefteq G$ lies in $X$, so it is $1$ or $X$; if $X\cap Y=X$ then $X\le Y$, so $X=Y$ by minimality of $Y$.

**(a)** $A\le KA\le AB$ (as $K\le AB$). By Dedekind's modular law, $KA=KA\cap AB=A(KA\cap B)$. $KA\cap B$ is normal in $G$ and contained in $B$, so it is $1$ or $B$. If it is $1$, then $KA=A$, so $K\le A$ and $K=A$ by minimality, a contradiction. Hence $KA\cap B=B$ and $KA=AB$. By symmetry ($A\leftrightarrow B$), $KB=AB$.

**(b)** By the remark, $K\cap A=K\cap B=1$. Also $A\ne B$ (if $A=B$ then $K\le AB=A$, so $K=A$), so $A\cap B=1$. Hence
$$K\cong K/(K\cap A)\cong KA/A=AB/A\cong B/(A\cap B)\cong B,$$
and similarly, using $KB=AB$, $K\cong KB/B=AB/B\cong A$.

**(c)** For normal subgroups $X,Y$, $[X,Y]\le X\cap Y$. So $[A,B]=[A,K]=1$: $A$ centralizes $B$ and $K$, hence centralizes $KB=AB\supseteq A$. Thus $A$ is abelian, and so is $B\cong A$. Since $A,B$ commute elementwise and $A\cap B=1$, $AB\cong A\times B$ is abelian. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2006s-02.title: Compare with Z[x]
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2006s-02.body:
**(a)** Let $F$ be the fraction field of $R$ (inside $\mathbb Q(x)$). Since $x^3,x^4\in R$, $x=x^4/x^3\in F$; also $\mathbb Z\subseteq R$, so $F\supseteq\mathbb Z[x]$ and hence $F$ contains the fraction field $\mathbb Q(x)$ of $\mathbb Z[x]$. Conversely $R\subseteq\mathbb Q(x)$ gives $F\subseteq\mathbb Q(x)$. So $F=\mathbb Q(x)$.

**(b)** Let $S$ be the integral closure of $R$ in $\mathbb Q(x)$. $x$ is a root of $T^3-x^3\in R[T]$, so $x\in S$, and $S\supseteq\mathbb Z[x]\supseteq R$. Conversely, an element of $S$ is integral over $R\subseteq\mathbb Z[x]$, hence over $\mathbb Z[x]$; since $\mathbb Z[x]$ is a UFD it is integrally closed in $\mathbb Q(x)$, so the element lies in $\mathbb Z[x]$. Hence $S=\mathbb Z[x]$.

**(c)** No. Suppose $R=\mathbb Z[g]$. Then $g\notin\mathbb Z$, so $d=\deg g\ge1$, with leading coefficient $c\ne0$. For $h=\sum_{i=0}^na_ig^i$ with $a_n\neq0$, the leading term is $a_nc^nx^{nd}\ne0$ ($\mathbb Z$ is a domain), so every nonzero element of $R$ has degree divisible by $d$. Since $x^3,x^4\in R$, $d\mid3$ and $d\mid4$, so $d=1$. But $R$ has no elements of degree $1$ — contradiction.

*Alternative:* the degree argument also shows $t\mapsto g$ gives $\mathbb Z[t]\cong R$; then $R$ would be a UFD, hence integrally closed, contradicting (b) since $x\in\mathbb Z[x]\setminus R$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2006s-03.title: Roots differ by roots of unity
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2006s-03.body:
**(a)** $f'(x)=nx^{n-1}$ with $n\ne0$ in $F$, so the only root of $f'$ is $0$, which is not a root of $f$ ($a\ne0$). Thus $f$ has $n$ distinct roots $b_1,\dots,b_n\in E$. The quotients $b_i/b_1$ satisfy $(b_i/b_1)^n=a/a=1$ and are distinct, so $E$ contains $n$ distinct $n$th roots of unity, i.e. the group $\mu_n(E)$ has order $n$. A finite subgroup of $E^\times$ is cyclic, so $\mu_n(E)$ has a generator $\varepsilon$, a primitive $n$th root of unity.

**(b)** If $\varepsilon\in F$, then all $n$th roots of unity $\varepsilon^j$ lie in $F$. Let $g$ be an irreducible factor of $f$ and $b_i$ a root of $g$. Then $F[b_i]$ contains $b_i\varepsilon^j$ for all $j$, which are all $n$ roots of $f$; so $F[b_i]=E$ and $\deg g=|F[b_i]:F|=|E:F|$. Writing $f=f_1\cdots f_m$ with $f_k$ irreducible, $n=\sum\deg f_k=m\,|E:F|$, so $|E:F|$ divides $n$.

**(c)** By (a), $\varepsilon\in E$, so $F\subseteq F[\varepsilon]\subseteq E$, and $E$ is a splitting field of $f\in F[\varepsilon][x]$ over $F[\varepsilon]$. By (b) applied over $F[\varepsilon]$, $|E:F[\varepsilon]|$ divides $n$, a power of $2$. It remains to show $|F[\varepsilon]:F|$ is a power of $2$, by induction on $n=2^k$. For $n=1$, $\varepsilon=1$. For $n\ge2$, $\delta=\varepsilon^2$ is a primitive $(n/2)$-th root of unity, so $|F[\delta]:F|$ is a power of $2$ by induction, and $\varepsilon$ is a root of $x^2-\delta\in F[\delta][x]$, so $|F[\varepsilon]:F[\delta]|\in\{1,2\}$. Multiplying degrees, $|F[\varepsilon]:F|$ and hence $|E:F|=|E:F[\varepsilon]|\,|F[\varepsilon]:F|$ are powers of $2$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2006s-04.title: Common invariant subspaces
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2006s-04.body:
**(a)** The characteristic polynomial $f$ of $A$ is real, monic, of odd degree $m$. Then $f(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$ and $f(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$, so by the intermediate value theorem $f$ has a real root, which is a real eigenvalue of $A$. (Alternatively, nonreal roots of $f$ come in conjugate pairs, so the number of real roots counted with multiplicity is odd.)

**(b)** Induction on $\dim V$; $\dim V=0$ is even.

*Case 1:* there is a subspace $0\ne W\ne V$ invariant under every $A_i$. The restrictions $A_i|_W$ and the induced operators on $V/W$ still commute pairwise and sum to $-I$; their characteristic polynomials divide that of $A_i$ (block triangular form), so they have no negative real eigenvalues. By induction $\dim W$ and $\dim V/W$ are even, hence so is $\dim V$.

*Case 2:* no such $W$ exists. Suppose $\dim V$ is odd. By (a) each $A_i$ has a real eigenvalue $r_i$, and $r_i\ge0$ by hypothesis. The eigenspace $W_i=\ker(A_i-r_iI)\ne0$ is invariant under every $A_j$ (since $A_jA_i=A_iA_j$). Hence $W_i=V$, i.e. $A_i=r_iI$. Then $-I=\sum A_i=(\sum r_i)I$, so $\sum r_i=-1<0$, contradicting $r_i\ge0$. So $\dim V$ is even. ∎
